chapter_theme: Poems 261-280 are the hero-stone and battlefield poems: laments for cattle-defenders who became stones, the victory feast of the raiders, the nochchi of the fort's defenders, single warriors against armies, and the old mothers and wives who measure a death by its honour and its cost.

261.reading: A poet sees the ever-open house of his dead lord, once loud with toddy bowls, endless rice and meat frying in ghee for newcomers, now as useless as a ferry on a dried river and as bare as a widow with shorn head, because the young spearman who brought back the cattle and was crowned with karanthai has become a hero-stone.
261.nuance: The address shifts in mid-poem from the poet's own eyes (சோர்க, என் கண்ணே) to the house itself (பயந்தனை... புல்என் றனையால்), so the house is mourned as a person who has lost her husband. Lines 11 and 12 (the unlearned bowmen, the owl's call) are compressed and their syntax is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the dead man is a cattle-recoverer crowned with karanthai, and the poem laments him as a hero-stone

comparisons.tenor: the lord's courtyard, now of no use
the hiss of meat frying in ghee

comparisons.vehicle: கொய்ம்மழித் தலையொடு கைம்மையுறக் கலங்கிய கழிகலம் மகடூஉப் போல
comparisons.tenor: the house stripped of its ornaments

262.reading: Draw the toddy, slaughter the ram, fill the leaf-roofed shed with fresh river sand: my lord is coming with the herd, having broken the enemy's front and guarded the rear, and those beside him are spent more than he.
262.nuance: The leader is both in front (முருக்கி) and behind (பின்நின்று): he breaks the enemy and then guards the retreat with the herd. Line 6 can be read as his companions being more worn than he, or gentler than he; either way the feast is ordered for them all.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord returns driving a captured herd, the cattle raid of vetchi

263.reading: A bard with a one-faced drum like an elephant's footprint is told not to pass without worshipping the stone on this road: it stands for the man who turned back the stolen herd, stood fast when the untrained youths fled, and, sunk in arrows, held the enemy like a dam against a killing flood.
263.nuance: The poem is an instruction to a passing performer: the dead man's stone has become a place of worship on the road, which is how a lament turns into a cult. Line 4 (வண்டுமேம் படூஉம், இவ் வறநிலை யாறே) is hard: it may mean the road through dry land where bees swarm at the garlanded stone, or a path of virtue.

thinai_evidence.note: the dead man turned back a driven-off herd: the deed of karanthai

comparisons.tenor: the warrior holding back the enemy

264.reading: On the gravelly ground they have heaped the cairn, crowned it with a red flower garland bound with split maral fibre and with peacock feathers, carved his name and set up the stone; will the bards' troupe still come today, not knowing that the noble man who drove off the enemy and brought back the cows with their calves is gone?
264.nuance: The grief is measured from the bards' side: the rite is complete (cairn, garland, feather, name, stone) but the news has not travelled, so the performers who lived on his giving are still on the road to him. The order of the rite in lines 1 to 4 is itself a record of how a hero-stone was made.

thinai_evidence.note: the dead man brought back the milch cows with their calves

265.reading: On the old gravelly battlefield far beyond the town, the cowherds have crowned you with a garland of venkai blossom tied with palmyra leaf, and you have become a stone, prince of swift horses; and with you have gone not only the wealth of the bards who lived in the shade of your feet but the victory that made elephant-riding kings shrink.
265.nuance: The cowherds, not kings or priests, perform the crowning, with flowers of the hill (venkai) and leaf of the palmyra: the stone belongs to the people he protected. The last lines make the loss double, patronage and conquest at once, so the dead man's giving and his fighting are one reputation.

thinai_evidence.note: the cowherds honour the dead man at his stone, which places him as the defender of their cattle

comparisons.tenor: the patron's feet that sheltered bards

266.reading: The poet asks Chenni, lord of a land whose watered fields stay green even when the rains fail, to remove at once, as a plea made in the assembly of the wise is answered, the poverty that has risen in his body, ruining his understanding and making him hide from the very guests he longed for.
266.nuance: The snail pair mating in the shade of a lily leaf at midday, in a drought, shows a land so well watered that even the weakest creatures prosper; the poet's own house is the one place in it where the guest is avoided. The comparison makes relief a matter of justice, as in a court, rather than of favour.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises a king's land and presses him for relief from poverty

comparisons.vehicle: சான்றோர் இருந்த அவையத்து உற்றோன் ஆசாகு என்னும் பூசல்
comparisons.tenor: the poet's plea to the king

269.reading: After the warrior, his hair wreathed with loose athiral buds sharp as a koel's beak, has drunk the warm liquor once or twice from a new bowl, the drummer comes asking for pressed toddy, and he is given instead, it is said, this dark-handled sword, which cut down the bowmen who had seized the herd and drove them back while the kites cried over them.
269.nuance: Who says 'take this' in lines 7 and 8 (என்ப, 'they say') and what 'this' is are not settled by the syntax; read with the closing words இக் கருங்கை வாளே, the feast's answer to a request for drink is the sword's deed. Avvaiyar's poem keeps the feast and the slaughter in one sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the feast follows a raid in which the sword beat back the karanthai men who tried to retake the herd

270.reading: Addressing the grey-haired mother of a great house, the poet says that even wheel-rolling emperors with drums and elephants meet in battle what they sought, and grieves while bidding her look at her son, who, after warriors stirred by the war drum fought a fearful battle, lies on the swords like a tree felled by an axe.
270.nuance: The poet's நோகோ யானே (I grieve) is set against நோக்குமதி நீயே (but you, look): the mother is asked to see valour where the poet sees loss. Lines 1 to 4 on the emperors are elliptical and their link to the son is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament over a warrior dead in a pitched battle, with nothing of cattle recovery that karanthai needs

comparisons.tenor: the son lying on the swords

271.reading: We once saw the bright nochchi leaves, grown where the ground never lacks water, worn as a girdle on the waists of jewelled women; now we have seen the same leaves, soaked in blood and shredded out of shape, carried off by a kite that took them for flesh, because the young warrior eager for battle wore them.
271.nuance: The warrior's death is never stated; it is told only through what happened to the leaf he wore, from women's ornament to carrion. The kite's mistake (ஊன்செத்து) makes the garland stand for his flesh.

thinai_evidence.note: the warrior wore nochchi, the flower of those who defend a fort

272.reading: The poet praises the nochchi, its clusters like strung sapphires, as the best loved of flowering trees: it gives shade, lies on the waists of bangled women in the guarded mansion, and, because the enemy breached the guarded wall, it also wins the honour of crowning the noble man who would not yield the town's outskirts.
272.nuance: The tree is addressed as a person with rights (கிழமையும் நினதே): its last and highest claim is to the head of the defender at the moment the wall falls. The colophon's falling in battle is implied by the breach, not stated.

thinai_evidence.note: the defence of a walled town, whose sign is the nochchi

273.reading: A wife cries that her husband's horse has not come while everyone else's horses have returned, and asks whether it has perished like a great tree that lies across the meeting of two great rivers.
273.nuance: She asks only about the horse; the rider's fate is left unspoken, and naming him as the one who gave her a son puts the household's future into the question. The tree across the confluence fits a horse (and rider) that blocked two converging armies.

thinai_evidence.note: the horse fought in a pitched battle and has not returned

comparisons.vehicle: இருபேர் யாற்ற ஒருபெருங் கூடல் விலங்கிடு பெருமரம்
comparisons.tenor: the horse that stood across the enemy's onrush

274.reading: The great warrior in blue waistband, flowered cloth and peacock-feather crown hurled his spear at the oncoming elephant; now, as the foes with spears came on with their horses, he seems ready to hurl himself too, and seizing with his hand, embracing, lifting with his shoulder's strength, he took it upon his body.
274.nuance: With his spear gone, the warrior turns himself into the weapon (தன்னும் துரக்குவன்). What he seizes in lines 6 and 7 (an enemy's spear, or an enemy) is not stated, and the last verb can mean taking it bodily or taking it into his body.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior facing elephants and horsemen in pitched battle

275.reading: His bent garland, his cloth of curling folds and his naming what he wanted as he went at the king all suit him: splitting the koovai so the ranks cried out, raising his spear at the front, crying 'hold here, hold here!' without guarding himself, his legs tangled in the guts of a chained elephant, he rushes like a cow to its calf toward the comrade who faced the first clash.
275.nuance: The simile of the cow running to its calf is a tender one inside a scene of entrails: the warrior's rush to his comrade is love, not only valour. Lines 3 and 4 (செற்றிய திணிநிலை, கூவை போழ்ந்து) are hard and the sense of the opening garland and cloth is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: a warrior challenging a king in open battle

comparisons.tenor: the warrior going to his comrade

276.reading: The beloved son of a red-skinned old woman, her white hair untended and her breasts dry and shrunk like dark seeds, became the ruin of a whole army, as a few drops of curd-starter flicked by a cowherd girl's nail turn a pot of milk.
276.nuance: The simile turns on size: a few drops change a whole pot. Taken from the dairy of mullai, it makes the hero's deed as quiet and certain as a daily chore, and sets the dried breasts of the mother against the milk.

thinai_evidence.note: one warrior against a whole army in battle

comparisons.vehicle: மடப்பால் ஆய்மகள் வள்உகிர்த் தெறித்த குடப்பால் சில்லுறை
comparisons.tenor: the one son who undid an army

277.reading: When the old woman with hair white as the down of a fish-eating heron heard that her son had killed an elephant and fallen, her joy was greater than on the day she bore him, and her tears outnumbered the drops that hang on the swaying bamboo after rain.
277.nuance: The thurai's name, joy and weeping together, is the poem's structure: one sentence for each. The bamboo after rain is an image of plenty, so even her tears are counted as abundance.

thinai_evidence.note: the son died in battle after killing an elephant

comparisons.vehicle: நோன்கழை துயல்வரும் வெதிரத்து வான்பெயத் தூங்கிய சிதரினும்

278.reading: Told by many that her son had broken and fled, an old woman with withered, veined arms swore in rage to cut off the breasts he had sucked, took a sword and searched the red field turning over the dead, and when she found her son lying hacked to pieces, she rejoiced more than on the day she bore him.
278.nuance: Her proof is in the wounds: a son cut to pieces (சிதைந்து வேறாகிய) could not have run, so the report of the many is refuted by what she sees. Her vow against her own breasts makes motherhood itself answerable for the son's courage.

thinai_evidence.note: a battlefield search by a mother for her son's body

279.reading: The poet, aghast, says this woman's resolve is fierce and worthy of an old warrior house: her elder kinsman died killing an elephant the day before yesterday, her husband died yesterday holding back the great herd, and today, hearing the war drum, she puts a spear in the hand of her only son, wraps him in white cloth, oils his tufted hair and sends him to face the battle.
279.nuance: கெடுக சிந்தை, the poet's opening curse on her (or his own) mind, is awe close to horror. The days are counted (மேல்நாள், நெருநல், இன்றும்) so the poem becomes a three-day ledger of loss; the only son (ஒருமகன் அல்லது இல்லோள்) is the last entry. Whether தன்னை here is her father or elder brother is not fixed by the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the excellence of a woman of an old warrior house, the mark of vaakai's muuthin mullai

280.reading: A wife beside her husband's wounded body lists the bad signs, the burning wounds, the bee buzzing at midnight, the lamps that go out, the owl's cry, the old woman's omen that does not come right, pities the drummer, bard and virali whose life here is over too, and says that for her, to sit like widows with shaven heads eating white water-lily seeds and think of the road he took will be harder still.
280.nuance: The first seven lines are a run of omens, each a short clause ending in a verb, so the poem enacts a night of watching. She foresees widowhood in the simile and judges it harder than his death. Line 12 (தொன்றுதாம் உடுத்த அம்பகைத் தெரியல்) is obscure.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife's lament at the death of her husband from wounds

comparisons.vehicle: சிறுவெள் ஆம்பல் அல்லி உண்ணும் கழிகல மகளிர்

links.note: Both address the dead lord's house with புல்என் றனையால் (you have become desolate) and set a widow beside it: 261 likens the house to a widow with shorn head, 250 shows the widow shorn and eating lily seeds inside it.
links.teaches: One formula serves two poets, and the widow sits once in a simile and once in the house, which shows that the empty hall and the widow's state were one picture of a lord's death, interchangeable as tenor and vehicle.

links.note: 261 likens the house to a கழிகலம் மகடூஉ with shorn head; in 280 the wife foresees becoming one of the கழிகல மகளிர் with shaven head.
links.teaches: In 261 the shorn widow is only an image for a ruined house; in 280 the wife speaks it of herself as her own future, so the pair shows the same stock figure moving from ornament to fate depending on who speaks.

links.note: 335 says the people know no god worshipped with poured paddy except the stone of the man who fell killing an elephant; 263 tells a passing bard not to go by such a stone without worship.
links.teaches: 335 states the creed of the hero-stone as a general fact of a small warrior land, and 263 shows it working as an obligation laid on travellers, so together they show the cult reaching beyond the dead man's village to the road.

links.note: Both describe the making of a hero-stone: 264's name carved, red flower garland bound with maral fibre and peacock feather; Akananuru 269's names washed, turmeric, and a karanthai garland tied with fibre on the stone by the road.
links.teaches: The akam poet borrows the puram rite almost item by item to fill the heroine's fear of the road, which shows that the hero-stone was a fixed, widely known ritual whose details an akam audience would recognise as danger without being told.

links.note: In 232 Avvaiyar asks whether the patron who would not accept a whole country will now accept toddy poured at his feather-crowned stone; in 264 the bards may still be coming to a patron who is now a stone.
links.teaches: Both poems turn on the reversal the stone makes in the gift relation: in 232 the giver becomes a receiver of offerings, and in 264 the receivers arrive to find no giver, so together they show that a patron's death was grieved as the end of a circuit of giving.

links.note: 221 ends நடுகல் ஆயினன் புரவலன் (the patron has become a hero-stone); 265 says கல்ஆ யினையே (you have become a stone) and adds that the bards' wealth went with him.
links.teaches: The formula 'he became a stone' is used of a crowned king in 221 and of a local cattle-defender in 265, which shows that the hero-stone honour, and the bards' claim on the dead, were not reserved for kings.

links.note: Kural 771 threatens enemies that many who stood before the lord now stand as stones; in 265 the stone is the hero's own, and the poet grieves that patronage and victory went with him.
links.teaches: The Kural's boast treats the hero-stone as the enemy's fate and a mark of the lord's might, while 265 shows the same stone from the side of those left behind, so the pair shows that the honour Valluvar's warrior wields as a threat was, for the bards, a loss of livelihood.

links.note: Naladiyar 287 says want takes away good nature and sharpness of mind; 266 names its poverty as அறிவுகெட நின்ற, which has ruined his understanding, and as making him hide from guests.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's maxim that poverty destroys the mind is given here as a poet's own testimony with a concrete symptom, hiding from the guest one longed for, which shows that the loss of hospitality was felt as the loss of reason itself.

links.note: Naladiyar 286 says the man who cannot give to those who come hungry had better leave his village; 266 asks the king to end such poverty quickly, as a plea in the assembly is answered.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar makes the poor host's shame his own to solve by leaving, while the Purananuru poet places the remedy on the king as a matter of justice, so the pair shows two answers to the same shame: private withdrawal and a public claim on the ruler.

links.note: Both are உண்டாட்டு feasts after a cattle raid: 262 orders toddy drawn and a ram killed for the returning lord, 269 shows the warrior drinking and answering the drummer's request with the sword's deed.
links.teaches: 262 is the feast prepared and 269 the feast in progress, and in both the drink is bound to the deed that earned it, which shows that the victory feast was a rite of reward rather than mere celebration.

links.note: Both set the nochchi on women's waists and on the defender's head: 271 ends with the garland bloodied and carried off by a kite, 272 with the tree's honour of crowning the man who would not yield.
links.teaches: The same pairing of girdle and battle garland yields lament in one poet and praise in the next, which shows that the thurai செருவிடை வீழ்தல் could be sung through the flower alone, with the warrior's death left wholly implicit.

links.note: Kural 774's hero sends his spear away with an elephant and laughs as he pulls one from his own body; 274's warrior hurls his spear at the oncoming elephant and, weaponless, takes the enemy's attack upon his body.
links.teaches: The Kural's couplet compresses a set scene that the Purananuru gives at length with dress and enemy horse, which shows that Valluvar's chapter on martial pride was built on stock battle episodes the audience already knew from heroic song.

links.note: Kural 69: the mother who hears her son called worthy rejoices more than when she bore him (ஈன்ற பொழுதின் பெரிதுவக்கும்); 277: the old mother's joy at hearing her son died killing an elephant is greater than on the day she bore him (ஈன்ற ஞான்றினும் பெரிதே).
links.teaches: The Kural keeps the heroic measure of a mother's joy but moves its object from a son's death in battle to his being called worthy, so the pair shows Valluvar civilising a formula of the battlefield into one of learning and character.

links.note: Kural 69's mother rejoices on hearing her son praised; 278's mother hears a report of his flight, refuses it, searches the field, and rejoices more than at his birth only on seeing his body.
links.teaches: Where the Kural makes a mother's greatest joy depend on what she hears said of her son, 278 makes hearsay the thing to be refuted by sight of the wounds, which shows that the heroic mother trusted only the body's evidence of honour.

links.note: Both are உவகைக் கலுழ்ச்சி poems about an old mother whose son died in battle, and both end on joy greater than on the day she bore him (ஈன்ற ஞான்றினும் பெரிது).
links.teaches: One closing formula carries two different plots, joy at good news in 277 and joy after a false report of flight is disproved in 278, which shows that the thurai fixed the ending and left poets free to vary the path to it.

links.note: 312 lists the duties: to bear and rear the son is the mother's, to make him a warrior the father's, to kill elephants the son's; in 279 the father is already dead and the mother herself arms and dresses her only son for battle.
links.teaches: 312's tidy division of duties breaks down in 279, where the mother takes over the father's task of sending the son out because the men are dead, which shows the ideal of the warrior mother under the pressure of successive losses.

links.note: In 86 a mother says her womb is like a den a tiger has left and her son will be found on the battlefield; in 279 a mother with one son sends him to the battle after husband and kinsman have fallen.
links.teaches: 86 gives the mother's own proud voice and 279 an onlooker's awe at the same type, which shows that the warrior mother was praised both from within and from outside, and that the onlooker felt the cost (கெடுக சிந்தை) the mother does not speak.

links.note: 280's widows eat the seeds of the small white water lily (ஆம்பல் அல்லி உண்ணும்); 250's widow is the wife 'of lily-seed food' (அல்லி உணவின் மனைவி) with hair cut and bangles removed.
links.teaches: The repeated detail of lily-seed food in two poets shows that the widow's diet was a fixed public mark of her state, so that in 280 the wife can foretell her whole future by naming what she will eat.

links.note: In 246 the queen rejects the widow's life of lily-food and gravel bed and chooses the pyre; in 280 the wife foresees that life and says it will be harder than even the present grief.
links.teaches: 246 treats widowhood as a choice to be refused by fire, while 280 accepts it as the expected course and judges it the heavier burden, so the pair shows that the widow's austerities were seen as harder than death by both speakers, though only a queen could choose against them.

new_concepts.gloss: the hero-stone set up for a warrior who fell, crowned, inscribed with his name and worshipped
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: நடுகல் in 261 line 15; the stone also in 263 line 8 (கல்லே), 264 line 4 (கல்லும்) and 265 line 5 (கல்ஆ யினையே)

new_concepts.gloss: widowhood and its marks: shorn head, ornaments put off, the austere diet
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: கைம்மை in 261 line 17; கழிகலம் மகடூஉ in 261 line 18 and கழிகல மகளிர் in 280 line 14

new_concepts.gloss: the state of helpless grief after a patron's or lord's death, and the lament that voices it
the gift a bard seeks from a patron, and the asking for it
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word: பரிசிலர் in 265 line 7; the colophon of 266 is பரிசில் கடாநிலை

source_issues: 271 and 272: the colophon thinai reads நொட்சி, a misprint for நொச்சி; copied as it stands in colophon, inferred thinai nochchi.
280: the colophon thurai reads ஆந்தப் பையுள், a misprint for ஆனந்தப் பையுள்; corrected in puram_thurai name, colophon_form keeps the misprint.
276: the poet's name reads மாதுரைப் பூதன் இளநாகனார்; மாதுரை is likely a misprint for மதுரை.
262: the colophon thurai's alternative is written தலை தோற்றமுமாம், for தலைத்தோற்றமும் ஆம்; normalised in puram_thurai name.

275: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line 1. Our line 1 (கோட்டம் கண்ணியும், கொடுந்திரை ஆடையும்) supplies the subjects that line 3 (ஒத்தன்று மாதோ, இவற்கே) completes, so it belongs to the poem; marked as it stands.
270 line 2 repeats purananuru:137 line 1 (இரங்கு முரசின், இனம்சால் யானை), flagged by show; read as a shared formula, not a corruption.
263: the poet is not recorded (poet None).
270: the colophon's thinai is karanthai, but nothing in the poem concerns the recovery of cattle; inferred pothuviyal.
